findings.source_passage: but the fear of this vast dumb brute of the sea, was chained up and enchanted in him; he had no voice, save that choking respiration through his spiracle, and this made the sight of him unspeakably pitiable; while still, in his amazing bulk, portcullis jaw, and omnipotent tail, there was enough to appal the stoutest man who so pitied.
findings.source_locator: paragraph describing the whale's agony in flight, after the bird simile
findings.why_it_matters: This passage is one of the most rhetorically distinctive in the chapter—the 'chained up and enchanted' formulation, the 'portcullis jaw,' and the paradox of pity-and-terror together are signature Melville voice and carry major interpretive weight about the mute suffering of the whale. The draft reduces it to 'He had no voice save that choking respiration through his spiracle,' erasing the bird simile, the 'chained up and enchanted' phrasing, and the tension between pity and dread entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full passage from 'So have I seen a bird' through 'enough to appal the stoutest man who so pitied,' or at minimum preserve 'chained up and enchanted,' 'portcullis jaw,' and the explicit paradox of simultaneous pity and terror.

findings.source_passage: for all his old age, and his one arm, and his blind eyes, he must die the death and be murdered, in order to light the gay bridals and other merry-makings of men, and also to illuminate the solemn churches that preach unconditional inoffensiveness by all to all.
findings.source_locator: paragraph after the blind bulbs are described
findings.why_it_matters: This is one of the most frequently cited passages in critical literature on Moby-Dick—the indictment of industrial whaling as murder in service of social hypocrisy, bridals contrasted with churches. It is entirely absent from the draft. Its loss is an interpretive catastrophe for this chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore this sentence verbatim or near-verbatim; it is irreplaceable and must appear after the description of the blind bulbs.

findings.source_passage: In that sloping afternoon sunlight, the shadows that the three boats sent down beneath the surface, must have been long enough and broad enough to shade half Xerxes' army. Who can tell how appalling to the wounded whale must have been such huge phantoms flitting over his head!
findings.source_locator: after the Job passage, before 'Stand by, men; he stirs'
findings.why_it_matters: This is a tonally and imagistically distinctive passage—the Xerxes comparison is a classic Melvillean sublime digression with both rhetorical and interpretive weight (the hunters as a vast imperial army). It is completely absent from the draft.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Xerxes' army image and the meditation on the whale's perspective of phantom shadows; this is a brief but signature passage that should not be cut.

findings.source_passage: "I tell ye what it is, men"—cried Stubb to his crew—"it's against my religion to get mad; but I'd like to eat that villainous Yarman—Pull—won't ye? Are ye going to let that rascal beat ye? Do ye love brandy? A hogshead of brandy, then, to the best man. Come, why don't some of ye burst a blood-vessel? Who's that been dropping an anchor overboard—we don't budge an inch—we're becalmed. Halloo, here's grass growing in the boat's bottom—and by the Lord, the mast there's budding. This won't do, boys. Look at that Yarman! The short and long of it is, men, will ye spit fire or not?"
findings.why_it_matters: Stubb's comic-hyperbolic harangue is a voice-establishing set piece—'burst a blood-vessel,' 'grass growing in the boat's bottom,' 'mast there's budding,' 'spit fire or not' are individually quotable comic inventions. The draft collapses the whole speech to a few fragments, losing the escalating absurdist comedy that defines Stubb's character voice.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore more of Stubb's speech verbatim, particularly 'burst a blood-vessel,' 'mast there's budding,' and 'will ye spit fire or not?'

findings.source_passage: "Oh! see the suds he makes!" cried Flask, dancing up and down—"What a hump—Oh, do pile on the beef—lays like a log! Oh! my lads, do spring—slap-jacks and quahogs for supper, you know, my lads—baked clams and muffins—oh, do, do, spring,—he's a hundred barreller—don't lose him now—don't oh, don't!—see that Yarman—Oh, won't ye pull for your duff, my lads—such a sog! such a sogger! Don't ye love sperm? There goes three thousand dollars, men!—a bank!—a whole bank! The bank of England!—Oh, do, do, do!—What's that Yarman about now?"
findings.why_it_matters: Flask's speech is a comic tour de force—'slap-jacks and quahogs,' 'such a sog! such a sogger!', 'pull for your duff' are distinctively voice-establishing. The draft reduces it to a two-sentence fragment losing nearly all of this signature comic texture.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'slap-jacks and quahogs,' 'such a sog! such a sogger!', and the full 'bank of England' riff at minimum.

findings.source_passage: Seems it credible that by three such thin threads the great Leviathan was suspended like the big weight to an eight day clock. Suspended? and to what? To three bits of board.
findings.source_locator: meditation on the suspended whale before the Job quotation
findings.why_it_matters: The rhetorical question-and-answer structure ('Suspended? and to what? To three bits of board') is a signature Melville prose rhythm and sets up the Job quotation. The draft compresses this to 'Suspended by three such thin threads to three bits of board!' losing the interrogative rhetorical shape.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full sentence sequence with its rhetorical question-and-answer rhythm before the Job quotation.

findings.source_passage: even so from the points which the whale's eyes had once occupied, now protruded blind bulbs, horribly pitiable to see. But pity there was none.
findings.source_locator: revelation of the whale's blind eyes
findings.why_it_matters: The sudden pivot 'But pity there was none' is rhetorically sharp and interpretively loaded—it snaps the reader from sympathy to the cold reality of the hunt. The draft uses 'pity there was none' but loses 'horribly pitiable to see' and the full sentence about knot-holes in oaks, which makes the pivot more powerful.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the full knot-hole-in-oak simile and 'horribly pitiable to see' before 'But pity there was none' to preserve the rhetorical effect.

findings.source_passage: turned up the white secrets of his belly; lay like a log, and died. It was most piteous, that last expiring spout. As when by unseen hands the water is gradually drawn off from some mighty fountain, and with half-stifled melancholy gurglings the spray-column lowers and lowers to the ground—so the last long dying spout of the whale.
findings.why_it_matters: The draft preserves the fountain simile but introduces it with quotation marks ('As when by unseen hands…') as if attributing it to a speaker rather than the narrator, which misrepresents the prose and weakens the elegiac register.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the quotation marks; render this as authorial narration, not dialogue.

summary: Three high-severity failures—the erasure of the 'chained up and enchanted / portcullis jaw' passage with its bird simile, the complete omission of the 'murdered to light gay bridals and solemn churches' sentence (the chapter's most-cited critical passage), and the absence of the Xerxes' army image—together with multiple medium-severity voice flattening of Stubb's and Flask's harangues and the Job sequence setup, require regeneration.
